title: The Riddle of His Time
subtitle: Kaspar Hauser, Germany, 1828–1833
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Warm melancholic documentary illustration, a Bavarian/Franconian town in the 1820s-1830s, muted amber gaslight and grey stone, overcast Central European light, precise period 1828-1833 detail, cinematic wide composition, fine film grain, no modern text, no signage, nothing graphic.
facts: Verified 2026-07-05 via WebSearch + direct Wikipedia fetch (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaspar_Hauser) plus CNN's 2024-09-21 report on the new DNA study. Appeared Nuremberg 26 May 1828, ~16yo, letter in hand (unsigned, claimed custody since Oct 1812, said he wished to be a cavalryman 'as his father was'). 1829: attacked/forehead wound, survived, claimed a hooded man told him 'you still have to die before you leave the city of Nuremberg.' Fatal stabbing: 14 Dec 1833, Ansbach Court Garden, lured with the promise of a purse, died 17 Dec (3 days later). A violet purse found at the scene held a pencilled note in Spiegelschrift (mirror writing): 'Hauser will be able to tell you quite precisely how I look... I come from... the Bavarian border... I will even tell you the name: M.L.Ö.' Epitaph (verified, Ansbach): 'Hic iacet Casparus Hauser, aenigma sui temporis...' — English rendering used here ('riddle of his time... birth unknown, death mysterious') is the standard translation. The 'stolen prince of Baden' theory was the dominant legend for ~200 years; a Sept 2024 mitochondrial-DNA re-analysis (hair samples, ancient-DNA-grade method) found NO match to House of Baden mtDNA, ruling out princely descent (Springer/CNN). This does NOT identify who he actually was, nor settle the stabbing: a 2005 forensic re-analysis could not rule out murder, suicide, or accidental self-injury while staging an attack — presented here as a genuinely open question, not resolved either way.

beats.vo: In May of eighteen twenty-eight, a teenage boy appeared in a town square in Nuremberg, Germany. He could barely speak. In his hand, an unsigned letter — no name, no home, no past.
beats.img: A cobblestone town square in a small Bavarian city in the 1820s, surrounded by tall narrow gabled townhouses, a single distant solitary teenage figure standing in the open square clutching a folded letter, overcast grey daylight, no visible face, no modern signage.

beats.vo: He learned to talk. Learned to write. And all of Europe began to whisper the same theory: that he was a stolen prince, hidden away since infancy to protect someone else's throne.
beats.img: A modest 1820s German study interior, an open handwriting workbook and inkwell on a wooden desk near a window, warm daylight, a sense of someone slowly learning to write, no people visible, quiet and hopeful.

beats.vo: In 1829 someone attacked him with a knife; he survived. In December of 1833, someone lured him to a garden with the promise of a purse — and stabbed him for real. He died three days later.
beats.img: A dark formal garden path in a small German city at dusk in December, bare trees, a wrought iron gate, a single dropped violet drawstring purse lying on frost-covered gravel, no people, no blood, somber and still.

beats.vo: In his purse, police found a note in mirror writing, from someone signing only M, L, period, O. It described Hauser precisely — and promised nothing else. His own epitaph reads: a riddle of his time. Birth unknown. Death mysterious.
beats.img: Close on an old pencilled note beside a small violet purse resting on a stone garden bench at dusk, the handwriting on the paper completely illegible, cold blue winter light, melancholy, no people.

beats.vo: For two hundred years, the prince theory held. Then in 2024, new DNA analysis ruled it out for good — his blood doesn't match the royal family it was supposed to hide. Which leaves everything else exactly where it started.
beats.img: A quiet Franconian churchyard at dusk with one weathered 19th-century gravestone among bare trees, soft fading light, peaceful and sad, no legible text on the stone, no people.
